title: MURPHY: Feedback-Aware GRPO with Retrospective Credit Assignment for Multi-Turn Code Generation
claim: Our method outperforms prior baselines across iterative self-correction turns, with the largest gains on harder problems.
layout: 3 panels side by side (Easy/Medium/Hard), grouped bars by iteration, delta labels above
description: Three side-by-side grouped bar charts titled Easy, Medium and Hard subset, sharing a legend at the top. The legend has five colors: gray Base, blue GRPO-MT, green μCode, orange ReVeal and red Murphy, which has a bold outline. In each panel the x-axis shows Reflexion iteration (Iter-1, Iter-3, Iter-5) and the y-axis shows accuracy, with a different range per panel. Each iteration group has five bars with black error bars. Bars rise with iteration count. The red Murphy bar is usually tallest. Small numbers above the Murphy bars give its margin over the best baseline. Green numbers are gains such as +4.38 and +4.20. A red -1.67 marks the one loss, at Medium Iter-1. The gap widens on Medium and Hard, so the eye goes to the red bars and the delta labels.
caption: Self-correction performance on LiveCodeBench-v6. Qwen3-4B with \method vs. four execution-feedback baselines (Base, GRPO-MT, $\mu$Code, ReVeal) on the Easy, Medium, and Hard subsets. Base, GRPO-MT, $\mu$Code, and \method are evaluated under the Reflexion framework [ref]; ReVeal is evaluated using its official generation-verification scaffold, which uses a method-specific prompt and parser. All methods are compared at 1, 3, and 5 inference turns. Bars show the mean and stdev across 3 runs. \method shows large gains on the Medium/Hard subset (+4.38/+4.20 at Iter-$5$), where self-correction matters more.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become a standard recipe for post-training LLMs on reasoning tasks, with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) emerging as a leading approach. However, GRPO and its variants are inherently single-turn: they optimize from terminal rewards on isolated prompt-response pairs, leaving them poorly suited to agentic settings where models must iteratively refine solutions in response to environmental feedback. We introduce MURPHY, a multi-turn extension of GRPO for self-correcting code generation. MURPHY constructs feedback-conditioned rollout trees in which failed candidate solutions are paired with executor feedback and expanded into subsequent turns, and propagates rewards backward through the tree so that later successful refinements credit earlier attempts that surfaced informative feedback. We study two propagation strategies, Max Reward (MARS) and Mean Reward (MERS), and introduce post-rollout pruning mechanisms that reduce multi-turn optimization cost. Across three code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench-v6) and two model families (Qwen3-1.7B/4B, OLMo-2-7B), MURPHY delivers up to 6% absolute pass@1 gains over the strongest prior multi-turn execution-feedback methods. Gains are largest on the Medium/Hard subset (+4.38/+4.20 at Iter-5), where iterative self-correction matters more.
